title: Mandarin Oriental is reborn, 12 years and a pandemic later
summary: The 275-room luxury hotel reopens its doors just across the street from its old home, this time as part of the Ayala Triangle development

items: The new Mandarin Oriental hotel in Ayala Triangle, Makati, officially opened on November 26, 2020, after delays due to the pandemic, fulfilling a promise made in 2014.
The new hotel, designed by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill in collaboration with Leandro V. Locsin Partners, features 275 rooms, significantly fewer than the original hotel's 413 rooms.
Ayala Land aims to position the Philippines as a luxury tourism destination by emphasizing Filipino culture and craftsmanship in the hotel's design, rather than imitating other Asian luxury markets.

MANILA, Philippines – When the last guests checked out of the Mandarin Oriental in September 2014, the hotel promised to be back in six years.
Makati would have to wait twice as long – with a pandemic in between that set back its original 2020 opening date – but the day has finally arrived.
On Thursday, November 26, Ayala Land opens the new Mandarin Oriental at Ayala Triangle, making good on a promise made more than a decade ago.

The original Mandarin opened on Makati Avenue in 1976, just in time for the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. Designed by National Artist for Architecture Leandro Locsin, it was among the first Mandarin Oriental hotels outside Hong Kong, arriving at a time when Makati was not yet the skyscraper-lined business district it is today.

That iconic structure has since been demolished, and in its place rises Park Central Towers, another Ayala Land development, billed as an ultra-luxury residential twin tower. (READ: Luxury condo resilience: Half of Ayala’s Laurean buyers staying despite pause)

Still, its successor, built just across the street, keeps a connection to the old Mandarin. American architectural firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill designed the new hotel in collaboration with Leandro V. Locsin Partners, the practice founded by the late architect.

blocks.caption: REINVENTION. The 275-room Mandarin Hotel in Ayala Triangle, Makati City is owned by Ayala Land Hospitality and managed by Mandarin Oriental Hotel Group. Ayala Land handout

blocks.text: The new Mandarin is considerably smaller, at 275 rooms compared with its predecessor’s 413. That was part of the plan from the beginning, when Ayala Land first announced the project in June 2014.

The return of the Mandarin is also part of Ayala Land’s continuing reinvention of Ayala Triangle. Once part of Nielson Airport, the property went on to first house the Makati Stock Exchange and has today evolved into a hub anchored by Ayala Triangle Gardens Towers, with upscale restaurants and landscaped gardens – and finally, a luxury hotel to round it all out.

With the Mandarin, Ayala Land is also making a wager on the Philippines’ place in Asia’s luxury tourism market. The company believes Filipino culture and creativity can be a selling point in their own right, rather than looking to Singapore, Hong Kong, or Bangkok for a blueprint.

Filipino art, craftsmanship, and design feature prominently throughout the property. Ayala Land said it was designed around the idea that “the Philippines need not imitate other luxury destinations to compete with them.”

In the first nine months of 2026, Ayala Land’s leasing and hospitality revenues grew 8% year-on-year to P37.8 billion. Recurring-income businesses also now account for a greater part of the company’s earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA), standing at 55% and up from 44% in the same period last year. – Rappler.com
